title: Introduction: Why the Biggest AI Model Isn't Always Best
text: Hello, I'm Vineet Kumar Sarawat. The biggest model is rarely the right model. Every AI product trades quality against speed and cost, and product managers make that call. Here is how to choose between models without guessing. Always pick the cheapest model good enough for the job. Bigger models are usually smarter, slower, and costlier. The right choice depends on the task, and you find it by testing, not by reputation. Here are the five levers: quality, response speed, token usage, infrastructure capacity, and cost.

title: The 5 Core Levers of Model Selection
text: Improving one usually moves another, so model selection is a balancing act. Cost follows tokens. Providers usually charge for the tokens you send in and the tokens the model writes back, and output often costs more. Long prompts, long documents, and long answers all add up. Multiply the cost of one request by your expected daily traffic, and check the result against what a user is worth. Speed has two parts: how long until the first words appear, and how long the full answer takes. Streaming makes a wait feel shorter. Larger models are usually slower, and long outputs take longer. title: Understanding Token Costs & Latency (Time to First Token)
text: Product, not a technical detail. Infrastructure capacity is the hidden constraint. Providers set rate limits, and traffic spikes can cause slowdowns or errors. If you host models yourself, you need enough hardware at peak, not just on average. Plan for peaks, add fallbacks, and know what happens when a model is unavailable. You have tactics to balance all this. Use a smaller model for easy tasks and a larger one for hard ones. Route each request to the right model. Shorten prompts, cache repeated answers, and limit output length. Often a mix beats any single model. So, how do you choose? Define the quality bar and the latency and cost budgets first.
